title: Minimum Sideway Jumps
statement:
A road has 3 lanes (numbered 1 to 3) and points `0, 1, ..., n`, where `obstacles` has length `n + 1`. If `obstacles[i]` is 1, 2 or 3, that lane is blocked at point `i`; if it is 0, point `i` is clear. Each point has at most one blocked lane, and points `0` and `n` are always clear.

A frog starts in lane 2 at point 0 and must reach point `n` in any lane. It has two kinds of moves:

- step forward from point `i` to point `i + 1` in the same lane, allowed only when that lane is not blocked at point `i + 1`;
- a **side jump**: switch to any other lane (not only a neighbouring one) while staying at the same point, allowed only when the destination lane is not blocked at that point.

Return the smallest number of side jumps needed to reach point `n`.
notes:
## Intuition

At every point the frog is in one of only three states: lane 1, 2 or 3. If we know the fewest side jumps needed to stand in each lane at point `i - 1`, we can work out the same three numbers for point `i`: stepping forward keeps the count, a blocked lane becomes unreachable, and any open lane can also be reached with one side jump from the cheapest open lane at that point. A brute force runs a shortest-path search over all `3(n + 1)` states; the three-number DP does the same work in one sweep.

## Approach

1. `dp[lane]` (lanes 0, 1, 2 in code for lanes 1, 2, 3) is the fewest side jumps to stand in that lane at the current point. At point 0 it is `[1, 0, 1]`: lane 2 is free, the others cost one jump.
2. For each next point `i`, step forward: the counts stay, except the `blocked` lane, which becomes `Infinity`.
3. Let `best` be the smallest count at point `i`. Every open lane may also be reached by one side jump from that lane, so `dp[lane] = min(dp[lane], best + 1)`.
4. After point `n`, return the smallest of the three counts.

## Example 1, step by step

`obstacles = [0, 1, 2, 3, 0]`, `dp = [1, 0, 1]`.

- `i = 1`, lane 1 blocked: `[∞, 0, 1]`, `best = 0`, stays `[∞, 0, 1]`.
- `i = 2`, lane 2 blocked: `[∞, ∞, 1]`, `best = 1`, lane 1 gets 2: `[2, ∞, 1]`.
- `i = 3`, lane 3 blocked: `[2, ∞, ∞]`, `best = 2`, lane 2 gets 3: `[2, 3, ∞]`.
- `i = 4`, clear: `best = 2`, lane 3 gets 3: `[2, 3, 3]`.

The answer is `min = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): constant work for each of the `n` points.
- Space: O(1): only three counts are kept.

## Pitfalls

- Mark the blocked lane as unreachable before computing `best`, so no side jump starts from or lands on it.
- Side jumps happen at the new point, after stepping forward; a frog whose lane is blocked ahead must have jumped at the previous point, which the previous point's update already allowed.
- Lanes in `obstacles` are 1-based while `dp` is 0-based: subtract 1, and treat 0 (no obstacle) as `blocked = -1`.
- Start with `[1, 0, 1]`, not `[0, 0, 0]`: the frog begins in lane 2 only.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp` | fewest side jumps to stand in each lane at the current point |
| `i` | the current point |
| `blocked` | 0-based index of the blocked lane at point `i`, or -1 if none |
| `best` | the cheapest lane at point `i` before side jumps |
| `lane` | the lane being updated |

narration.2: At point 0 the frog stands in lane 2 for free; lanes 1 and 3 cost one side jump.
narration.3: Move the three counts forward one point at a time.
narration.4: Turn the obstacle's 1-based lane into a 0-based index (-1 when the point is clear).
narration.6: Stepping forward into a blocked lane is impossible, so that lane becomes unreachable.
narration.8: Find the cheapest lane to stand in at this point.
narration.9: Consider side-jumping into each lane at this point.
narration.10: The blocked lane cannot be a landing spot.
narration.11: Either keep the forward count or side-jump from the cheapest lane for one more jump.
narration.15: After the last point, the frog may finish in any lane; take the cheapest.
